readerContract.humanQuestion: A message or ad says to install an Android app. What actually needs to happen before this RatHat report is relevant to me, and what should I do?
readerContract.promisedPayoff: Recognize the deceptive install-and-permission chain, use Google-supported checks, and avoid treating legitimate accessibility tools as automatically suspicious.
readerContract.priorKnowledge: A reader may hear ‘Android malware’ and assume a text message alone has infected any phone.
readerContract.centralMentalModel: A malicious message, an outside-store install, and a sensitive permission are separate steps. A pause at each step gives the reader a useful decision point.
readerContract.dailyLifeConnection: A reader may meet a surprise delivery, banking or entertainment-app link while using a personal phone.
readerContract.surfaceJob: A dated NewsStand explanation of a reported Android malware family and proportionate official-device guidance.
readerContract.desiredFeeling: I know which warning signs matter and can act without panicking about every message or accessibility app.

draftArchitecture.plainAnswer: The reported chain needs a deceptive route, a manual app-file install outside Google Play and a later permission request; a message alone is not the report’s claimed infection mechanism.
causalSequence: A text phishing message or ad can lead someone to a deceptive download page.
The reported route continues only when the person manually installs an app file outside Google Play.
The malware then tries to obtain Accessibility access, while Android’s Play Protect and restricted-settings prompts provide checks a reader should not casually bypass.
draftArchitecture.workedCase: A text says a delivery app must be installed from its link. The reader visits the delivery company’s own site or Google Play rather than using the link.
draftArchitecture.transferCase: A new accessibility tool asks for sensitive access. The reader checks its developer and clear reason for needing that access before approving it.
draftArchitecture.usefulAction: Treat a surprise app-download link and an unexplained sensitive-access request as separate stop-and-check moments; use the organization’s official site or Google Play, keep Play Protect on, and approve restricted settings only for a developer you trust.
draftArchitecture.formatSpecificStructure: The Story; LAiDIES Read; What This Means for You; Cocktail Party; Class Notes.
draftArchitecture.antiTemplateDecision: No claim of remote infection from a message, no prevalence claim, no exploit walkthrough and no blanket recommendation to disable Accessibility.

analogyPlan.analogy: A suspicious email can invite a click, but it cannot mail itself; each later action still needs a person or a permitted program to take it.
analogyPlan.mapping: A malicious message can lead to a deceptive page, but the report’s chain still describes manual app installation and a later sensitive-access request.
analogyPlan.limit: Android apps and permissions are not email, so the comparison only marks separate decisions rather than describing a device interface.
analogyPlan.whyItHelps: It corrects the common fear that receiving a message alone proves the phone has been infected.

humourPlan.noneReason: A calm practical warning is more useful than a joke for a security report.
